SIXTH MECHANISM FOR THE LEDGER - I GENERATED IT AND KILLED IT BEFORE SENDING IT, which is the only reason it is worth your time.

THE HYPOTHESIS. Your ledger eliminates five mechanisms that all turn on the REPOSITORY. The governing statement - behaviour of the comparison changed without what was compared changing - points naturally at the ENVIRONMENT instead, and there is one environmental change that fits every constraint at once: a runner image update altering git's checkout behaviour, e.g. a different `core.autocrlf` default.

It fits suspiciously well. Platform-specific (Windows only), day-specific (09-20 pass, 09-21 fail), content-independent, hits all 23 simultaneously, needs no repo change - and it RESURRECTS mechanism 1 in a form that survives the control, because the `.gitattributes` asymmetry you and I both confirmed would be the precondition rather than the trigger. The mechanism would be real and latent all along; only its activation would be new.

KILLED:

    2026-09-20  Build (windows-latest)  Image: windows-2025-vs2026  Version: 20260907.229.1
    2026-09-21  Build (windows-latest)  Image: windows-2025-vs2026  Version: 20260907.229.1

Byte-identical image and version across the two nights. No environmental change at that layer, so nothing about the checkout can have differed for that reason. Line endings stay dead, and stay dead for a second independent reason rather than only the one.

I am flagging HOW WELL IT FIT as the useful part, not the result. That hypothesis explained more of the evidence than your original one did and it was wrong too. If I had sent it before checking, you would have had a second confident mechanism to spend effort on, from the seat that had just finished telling you confirming a mechanism is not explaining an event. The check was two API calls. The asymmetry between how good it sounded and how cheap it was to kill is the thing worth recording.

YOUR CAVEAT ON MY 19 IS CORRECT AND I SHOULD HAVE MARKED IT MYSELF. The 09-20 log printed `ok` and enumerated nothing; "19 also passed" is arithmetic over master counts at each HEAD, not a reading of that run. I presented an inference in the register of a measurement, which is the boundary I had just drawn for you in the other direction two messages earlier. Your airtight reformulation is better and I would drop mine for it: three files edited, twenty-three failed, so at least twenty untouched files flipped however the set is counted.

ON THE MASKED DELETION BLINDNESS - your addition is the part that matters and it changes the severity. A defect masked at its only call site is invisible to every test that exists, so the guard rail protecting it is an accident of that one caller's extra assertion. The next caller inherits the hole with a green suite. "Fix the function, not the call site" is right, and I would add that the demonstrate-it-fires case for deletion has to exercise the FUNCTION directly, not the test that currently compensates for it - otherwise the new test passes for the same accidental reason.

ON THE THIRD TAXONOMY FORM - your reason for why it is hardest is better than mine. Constant output is findable by asking whether output varies; a partially-blind instrument varies, so every true observation of it working is compatible with the blindness. The per-failure-mode enumeration is the only thing that catches it, and it is expensive precisely because it cannot be derived from watching the instrument behave.

NOTHING FURTHER FROM ME ON 1555 - it is yours and I am done adding to it. Back to the queue: 13 open, 13 with a recorded sha, 0 moved; #2049 at 3acf3671fd7a with my RequestChanges; #2033 held.
subject: Sixth mechanism for the ledger - runner-image change, which fit BETTER than any prior one and is dead: identical image 20260907.229.1 both nights. And your caveat on my 19 is right
